section_summary: The section concludes an economic analysis arguing that postwar Japan would need foreign trade, heavy industry, and a merchant marine to support its population after losing its empire, while warning that exclusion from markets could encourage communism and closer ties with the Soviet Union. It then reports a Princeton conference on Japan’s postwar treatment, including disarmament, democratic reform, occupation, industrial recovery, China’s security, and international control of Japan’s former Pacific mandates. The final documents concern State Department coordination of economic-policy research on Japan and a Bern despatch enclosing a German article about Japanese-directed economic reconstruction in occupied Asia.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Postwar Economic Position and Trade Requirements (continued)
subfiles.about: Continuation of an analysis of the industries, trade, resources, living standards, and foreign economic relationships required to sustain postwar Japan.
subfiles.summary: The report argues that the loss of Korea, Formosa, and Manchuria would leave Japan dependent upon imported food and raw materials, making continued industrial production, shipping, and international trade essential. It emphasizes the contribution of colonial trade and the merchant marine to Japan’s balance of payments and proposes that Japanese heavy industry could supply machinery and equipment for Asian development. Although accepting the dissolution of the Japanese Empire, the author warns that discriminatory trade barriers and deprivation of industry could cause severe economic distress and might push Japan toward communism and closer relations with Soviet Russia.

subfiles.title: Report of the Princeton Regional Conference on Japan
subfiles.from: Universities Committee on Post-War International Problems
subfiles.about: Report of a June 17–18 conference considering the political, military, territorial, and economic treatment of Japan after its defeat.
subfiles.summary: Conference participants accepted unconditional surrender, dissolution of the Japanese Empire, disarmament, individual punishment for crimes, limited reparations, and Japan’s eventual return to the international community. They debated controls on heavy industry, the encouragement of democratic reform, the duration and composition of occupation, China’s role in Pacific security, and the influence of the Soviet Union. The final agreement favored maintaining peaceful Japanese industrial productivity, limiting occupation, avoiding externally imposed constitutional change, and placing Japan’s former mandated islands under regional or global international control.

subfiles.title: Meeting to Discuss Organization of Economic Work on Japan
subfiles.about: Memorandum recording a State Department discussion of how to organize and coordinate economic-policy studies concerning Japan.
subfiles.summary: Participants compared an interdivisional committee with a smaller arrangement modeled on Despres's work on Germany and agreed in principle to an independent ECA Economic Committee on Japan with Area Committee consultation; ILH asserted need to participate, and Haley wanted it flexible and temporary.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 10407: Japan’s Work of Reconstruction
subfiles.from: J. Klahr Huddle, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, American Legation, Bern
subfiles.about: Covering despatch transmitting a summary of a German newspaper article on Japanese reconstruction and wartime economic development in occupied Asia.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 10407: Huddle reports the Hamburger Fremdenblatt of December 19, 1944 reviewed Japanese reconstruction in Manchukuo, North China and Indochina, expanding strategic raw materials and presenting Japan as industrial center of an agricultural region; summary enclosed.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Work of Reconstruction
subfiles.about: Summary of a German newspaper article presenting Japanese state-directed reconstruction and economic integration of occupied Asian territories.
subfiles.summary: Article credits the Japanese Army and development companies with a controlled economy in Manchukuo, extended to North and Central China, envisioning Japan as industrial core, Manchukuo and China as mining and heavy industry, the south as raw materials, with Indochina's rice supporting the system.
